title: Addressing Oxide Shell Formation in Harmonic Zinc Alloys for Improved Mechanical Integrity
content: Zinc and its alloys have attracted considerable interest in biomedicine, particularly for biodegradable implants such as bone fixation devices and vascular stents [1]. Zinc’s biocompatibility, moderate degradation rate, and essential role in physiological processes make it a promising alternative to traditional metallic biomaterials. For load-bearing applications, these materials must achieve tensile strengths above 300 MPa, elongation above 8%, and controlled corrosion rates to ensure both structural integrity and gradual biodegradation [2]. However, conventional zinc-based materials often fall short in mechanical strength and ductility, limiting their potential in these applications [3]. To overcome these limitations, powder metallurgy offers the ability to engineer novel microstructures with enhanced properties. One such approach is the development of harmonic structures, where hard and soft regions are strategically distributed throughout the material. When stress is applied, the softer regions deform first, generating dislocations that accumulate at the interfaces between the soft and hard zones. This accumulation leads to internal back and forward stresses, effectively enhancing resistance to deformation. As a result, hetero-deformation-induced strengthening and hardening improve the overall mechanical performance. A thorough understanding of the interactions at these interfaces is crucial for optimizing material design, as the balance between strength and ductility is key to ensuring superior performance [4-8].
